title: Decoding Signals from David Coleman and Chester Finn, Directors of the Common Core Chorus (Opinion)
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood reacts to an EdWeek admission that the Common Core architects left curriculum and instruction deliberately blank, and warns that the gap is now being filled by commercial, Core-aligned materials and scripted methods. He argues that publishers treat every child as if dyslexic, and that a narrow Science of Reading orthodoxy is deprofessionalising teachers by substituting teacher-proof scripts for their judgment. Drawing on an early-1990s scripted phonics site visit and a year consulting in Chicago schools under reconstitution threat, he describes classrooms driven by Scantron cycles, reteaching to the test and what Perkins called the fingertip effect, where handing teachers a tool is mistaken for teaching them to use it. He contrasts this with professional learning communities supported by research on teacher collaboration. He ends by urging reading educators to build an SoR 2.0 based on dialogic knowledge building inside professional practice.
points: The Core left materials and methods blank while building an accountability loop, and commercial publishers have filled that space with scripted, teacher-proof programs.
Underwood challenges applying dyslexia-grade phonics to every first grader for 25 minutes a day, since dyslexia is real but not an epidemic.
The fingertip effect: giving teachers a tool is not the same as teaching them to use it, so administrators wrongly blame teachers when tools fail.
His Chicago account shows how accountability pressure produces Scantron-driven reteaching and low expectations in under-resourced schools.
He proposes SoR 2.0, built on teacher and researcher collaboration in professional learning communities rather than mandated methods.
quotes: But they intentionally left blank all of the space taken up by curriculum and instruction and deliberately stayed silent.
Commercial publishers have taken to treating all children as if they have dyslexia. If they don’t, they suffer the fate of Lucy Calkins.
But dyslexia is not an epidemic. Thinking that first-grade teachers must teach the same phonics that you would use with a dyslexic child to every child in class for 25 minutes per day is problematic.
Administrators whose days are spent outside of classrooms sometimes assume that if they provide teachers a tool, teachers will use it. If they fail to produce, it becomes their fault.
Let’s start SoR 2.0 and locate it in dialogic knowledge building inside professional practice involving teachers and researchers in planful collaboration in every LEA.
